claims.statement: The Pay Transparency Directive requires objective gender-neutral job evaluation, worker information, and management-confirmed reporting, while allowing recognition of voluntary transparency; the founder can acquire a defensible control point through reciprocal contributor contracts under which employers supply pseudonymized job and pay records in exchange for a regional benchmark and an independent job-value map.

EU pay-transparency rules are taking effect in 2026 and require salary ranges, worker access to comparable pay information, and employer reporting; for reporting employers, an unexplained average gender difference of at least 5% in a worker category that is not corrected within six months triggers a joint pay assessment, making remediation payroll, legal process, and delayed hiring measurable losses.

Employers with 250 or more workers must begin annual reporting by 7 June 2027, those with 150-249 workers report every three years from that date, and all employers face applicant and worker information duties; the payer is a mid-market employer's HR, compensation, legal, internal-audit, or payroll function when designing pay ranges, answering a worker request, or preparing reporting.

contrary_evidence: Employers with 100-149 workers do not face directive-level reporting until 2031 unless national law accelerates it, and smaller employers may buy only minimal legal templates.

Established compensation consultancies, payroll processors, and HR platforms can add pay-gap analysis, while employers may refuse to contribute data to a shared benchmark even under strong privacy controls.

economics.acquisition_route: Recruit a cohort of ten Polish employers in one data-rich sector through a payroll bureau or employer association; execute a narrow data-contribution agreement, produce a blind task-and-pay benchmark, and run a paid pre-reporting assessment before building software.
economics.founder_net_worth_path: A cooperative serving 1000 Central European employers at an assumed 20000-60000 PLN annual membership could become a profitable regional compensation-data asset; expansion depends on repeatable job normalization and trusted governance rather than bespoke consulting hours.
economics.founder_time: Approximately 12-18 founder hours per week for data modeling, governance, and channel partnerships; employment counsel and worker-representation facilitation are contracted.
economics.gross_margin_basis: Preliminary 80-90% gross margin for recurring benchmark access after secure ingestion and taxonomy are built, with legal review and bespoke joint assessments priced separately.
economics.payback: An employer pays if the membership and assessment cost less than external consulting, reactive legal work, mispriced remediation, or repeated recruiter benchmarking; avoided liabilities are uncertain and should not be promised.
economics.pricing: Assumed 20000-60000 PLN annual membership by headcount, 5000-20000 PLN for secure onboarding, and 15000-75000 PLN for a joint-assessment evidence pack with employment counsel excluded or passed through.
economics.retention_or_repeat: Pay, headcount, roles, variable compensation, and national rules change each year; worker requests, hiring ranges, and scheduled reporting create ongoing use.

fingerprint.compounding_advantage: A privacy-governed regional graph linking actual tasks, skills, responsibility, working conditions, pay components, remediation choices, and later outcomes across employers.
fingerprint.customer: EU employers with 150-2000 workers, especially Central European firms lacking mature compensation analytics, plus payroll and employment-law partners.
fingerprint.distribution_mechanism: Payroll bureaus, employer associations, employment-law firms, auditors, and workers' representative advisers recruit closed cohorts that contribute data under reciprocal rules.
fingerprint.offer_and_business_model: A reciprocal benchmark cooperative that normalizes work value, identifies unsupported pay differences, and produces worker-request and reporting evidence; sold as membership plus scoped assessment.
fingerprint.payer_and_paid_event: An employer pays from HR, compensation, legal, audit, or payroll budget when setting salary ranges, receiving an information request, finding a 5% category gap, or approaching a reporting date.
fingerprint.problem_trigger: An employer must justify pay for work of equal value but lacks a defensible regional task benchmark and cannot rely on job titles alone.

founder_fit: Statistical matching, privacy-preserving aggregation, and bias diagnostics align with the founder's data-science background.
Channel sales through payroll bureaus and associations reduce repeated cold networking and personal-brand demands.
A ten-employer cohort can be validated part-time with limited capital and external legal review.
risks: A re-identification or payroll-data breach would be highly damaging and could trigger GDPR liability.
A benchmark can document market practice without proving legal equality of work, so overclaiming could harm clients.
National transposition may diverge enough that one regional methodology is not portable.

structure.control_point: Employer contribution agreements and a governed cross-company job-value and pay-component taxonomy.
structure.critical_dependency: Enough employers must contribute comparable granular data without creating unacceptable privacy, labor-relations, or antitrust risk.

thesis: Pay transparency shifts the hard problem from calculating a gap to defending why different roles are or are not equal in value. A closed employer cooperative can control the scarce regional task and compensation benchmark, giving members auditable comparisons while compounding remediation outcomes that a one-company HR tool or generic salary survey cannot see.
title: Pay-Equity Benchmark Cooperative
uncertainties: Will Polish and neighboring employers contribute task-level pay data before their first mandatory reports?
What minimum cohort size produces a useful benchmark without exposing individuals or employers?
Can worker representatives and employment counsel accept a shared job-value taxonomy as evidence rather than advocacy?
